summaries.summary: Adversarial examples threaten high-dimensional ML systems and prompt questions about brittle learning, while human perception is regarded as the computer-vision robustness gold-standard.
Humans can be fooled by optical, auditory, and other illusions, but these are generally viewed as isolated examples far from everyday instances.
This work studies human natural-speech susceptibility to adversarial attacks, focusing on the density of McGurk-effect illusions and their variable strength.
Dense human illusionable instances could create security risks by letting agents with screen access obfuscate or alter perceived auditory messages.
The authors distinguish McGurk misdubbed-audio illusions from ML adversarial examples and note little systematic study of illusion density in everyday instances.
The setup defines McGurk illusions f(x′,x) with unmodified audio x and visual dubbing x′, and calls tokens illusionable if perception changes for a significant fraction.
Phoneme-level experiments analyze McGurk illusions for phonemes, words, and sentences to obtain a lower bound on illusionable natural speech density.
The authors find many everyday words can become McGurk-style illusions, these persist in natural sentences, and natural-language-modeling features predict illusionability.
The authors tested vowel and consonant pairs with 10 labelers, finding vowels hard to confuse but several illusionable consonants dependent on speaker and listener.
They sampled 200 unique words from Project Gutenberg's 10,000 most common words, tested 147 candidates on 20 naive subjects, and allowed up to three plays.
Illusory videos caused 24.8% average miscomprehension, a relative 148% increase, with 5.1% unclear correct answers and 17% of words exceeding 30% error increases.
A ridge-regression model used 30 positional phoneme features, [0.1, 1, 10, 100] regularization, 85%:15% splits, and yielded 91.1±0.6% training and 44.6±28.9% test correlations.
The final word-level model achieved 57% out-of-sample correlation between predicted and observed illusionabilities using averaged coefficients from trials excluding each word.
Predicted word illusionability was calibrated, with mean empirical values 0.04, 0.14, 0.27, and 0.50 across increasing prediction intervals.
The sentence experiment sampled 300 Little Women sentences, perturbed 32, tested 1306 Turkers, omitted 112 (8.6%), and found 32.8% miscomprehension, a relative 145% increase.
A sentence-level model achieved 33% out-of-sample correlation using maximum word illusionability, while Project Gutenberg top 36.7k word frequencies did not improve it.
Word-level McGurk illusionability is significantly higher than sentence-level illusionability, though significant sentence-level illusionability remains.
Future work includes better sentence-level models, McGurk security risks, audio-to-video-dub systems, and robust rephrasing that preserves meaning.
Understanding human nonrobustness may improve ML robustness, including automatic speech recognition, McGurk effects, reduced vocabularies, and human anticipation of machine misclassification.
The authors call for reexamining human perception robustness as ML weakness-probing tools develop and announce preliminary audio-only illusion results.
The 2018 “Laurel”/“Yanny” clip inspired five additional examples, including 10 “worlds”/“yikes” versions with person-dependent interpretation-switching thresholds.
From 5000 words, 50 spectrogram-matched Google Cloud Text-to-Speech API candidates were damped and slowed 1.3-1.9x, with five evaluated on 15 individuals.
The work suggests subtle, learnable perturbations alter human perception for a significant fraction of natural speech and may pose security risks.
The authors hope future work discovers, generates, and quantifies illusions, models natural-language illusionability, improves robustness, and probes human cognition and ML systems.
Support came from NSF award AF:1813049, ONR award N00014-18-1-2295, and Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI, under Stanford IRB Protocol 46430.
